title: The Fifteen-Hundredth Term
statement: Let $a_1 < a_2 < a_3 < \dots$ be all the positive integers whose base-$2$ representation, written without leading zeros, has strictly more digits equal to $1$ than digits equal to $0$. Find the remainder when $a_{1500}$ is divided by $1000$.
hints: Group the terms of the sequence by their number of binary digits. Write a number as a leading $1$ followed by $d$ free digits, and work out how many $1$s those $d$ digits must contain.

The $d$ free digits must contain $j$ ones with $2j \ge d$. Counting these strings is a sum over the upper half of row $d$ of Pascal's triangle, so use the symmetry of binomial coefficients to evaluate it. Once the length of $a_{1500}$ is known, find its digits from left to right by counting how many valid numbers have a $0$ in each position.

The half-row sums show that $1199$ terms have at most $11$ digits, so $a_{1500}$ is the term of rank $301$ among the $12$-digit terms. These are the numbers whose last $11$ digits contain at least $6$ ones. At each position, with $m$ digits after it and $r$ ones still needed, a $0$ leaves $\sum_{j \ge r} \binom{m}{j}$ completions. If the current rank is at most this count, the digit is $0$. Otherwise the digit is $1$, and you subtract the count from the rank and reduce $r$ by $1$. Run this procedure through all $11$ positions and convert the resulting binary string.
solution:
A number with $d+1$ binary digits is a leading $1$ followed by $d$ free digits. If $j$ of the free digits are $1$, it has $j+1$ ones and $d-j$ zeros. It is a term iff $j+1>d-j$, i.e. $2j\ge d$. So the number of terms with $d+1$ digits is
$$T_d=\sum_{2j\ge d}\binom dj.$$
For odd $d$, symmetry gives $T_d=2^{d-1}$. For even $d$, $T_d=\frac{2^d+\binom d{d/2}}{2}$. For $d=0,\dots,10$ this gives
$$1,1,3,4,11,16,42,64,163,256,638,$$
with sum $1199$. Also $T_{11}=1024$ and $1199+1024\ge1500$. Hence $a_{1500}$ has $12$ digits, and it is the $301$st term with $12$ digits. These terms are those whose $11$ free digits contain at least $6$ ones.

Let $N(m,r)$ be the number of binary strings of length $m$ with at least $r$ ones, with $N(m,0)=2^m$. Build the free digits from the left. Suppose the required rank is $R$, $r$ more ones are needed, and $m$ digits follow the current position. Placing $0$ here leaves $N(m,r)$ completions, and these come before all those with a $1$ here. So the digit is $0$ if $R\le N(m,r)$. Otherwise the digit is $1$, $R$ becomes $R-N(m,r)$ and $r$ becomes $\max(r-1,0)$. Starting from $R=301$, $r=6$:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}
\text{position} & m & r & N(m,r) & R & \text{digit}\\ \hline
1&10&6&386&301&0\\
2&9&6&130&301&1\\
3&8&5&93&171&1\\
4&7&4&64&78&1\\
5&6&3&42&14&0\\
6&5&3&16&14&0\\
7&4&3&5&14&1\\
8&3&2&4&9&1\\
9&2&1&3&5&1\\
10&1&0&2&2&0\\
11&0&0&1&2&1
\end{array}$$

So $a_{1500}=(101110011101)_2=2048+512+256+128+16+8+4+1=2973$. This has $8$ ones and $4$ zeros, as required.

The remainder on division by $1000$ is $973$.
